Kombine · 35 models · 30 anchor pairs

When two models invent the same thing

Give 2,070 inventions the same starting pair of concepts and models rediscover each other's work. An inventive multiple is two models that invented the same entity by re-using the same properties — the model analogue of Newton and Leibniz. Every one found in the benchmark is catalogued below, and under each one, the models that saw the same two concepts and invented something else — no cluster ever takes the whole pool. Often those models share the cluster's abstraction and still build something different on it: the anchors can force the schema, the invention stays the model's. The abstraction is shown for reading; it plays no part in the criterion.

Each cluster leads with what its models actually say about the invention — the (relation, object) slots that recur across them, counted over all 35 models that answered the item, however each one worded it. The coined names differ far more than the properties do. Individual inventions, in full, are one click away.

A pair qualifies when the two inventions re-use at least τ = 2 of the same properties — every triple reduced to its “relation object”, the coined name dropped, any property whose object is one of the anchors dropped, matched one-to-one at cosine ≥ 0.545 (calibrated so that one property pair in 400 from unrelated inventions clears it). The name is never an input: of the 753 pairs that coined the identical name, 21% qualify.
